clinicalPearls: Bardet-Biedl syndrome is a multisystem ciliopathy whose cardinal features are rod-cone dystrophy, obesity, postaxial polydactyly, learning difficulties, hypogonadism and renal anomalies
Atypical cases lack one or more cardinal features or show unusual combinations, making clinical diagnosis difficult
More than twenty BBS genes are recognised, most encoding components of the BBSome or its chaperonins that mediate ciliary transport
In some families inheritance is oligogenic, with variants at a second locus modifying penetrance or severity (so-called triallelic inheritance)
A single heterozygous variant is generally insufficient, but modifier alleles can influence expression
Renal disease is a major cause of morbidity and may be the presenting or dominant feature in atypical cases
Because features emerge over time, diagnosis is often delayed and requires reassessment as the phenotype evolves
reference.pathophysiology: Bardet-Biedl syndrome results from dysfunction of the BBSome, a protein complex, and its associated chaperonins that together traffic membrane proteins into and along the primary cilium. Because the primary cilium is a near-ubiquitous sensory and signalling organelle, its impairment affects many tissues, producing the retinal photoreceptor degeneration, hypothalamic dysregulation of appetite, limb patterning defect, gonadal and renal maldevelopment and cognitive effects that define the syndrome. Most cases follow autosomal recessive inheritance, but in some families the phenotype is modulated by additional variants at a second BBS locus (oligogenic or triallelic inheritance), which helps explain the variable expression and the atypical presentations in which one or more cardinal features are absent or a single organ dominates.
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography for rod-cone dystrophy
Renal ultrasound and function testing for structural and functional kidney disease
Radiographs of the hands and feet to detect postaxial polydactyly
Metabolic and endocrine assessment for obesity, diabetes and hypogonadism
Broad Bardet-Biedl / ciliopathy gene panel or exome analysis with attention to oligogenic contributions
redFlags: Progressive renal impairment towards end-stage disease
Complications of obesity such as type 2 diabetes and hypertension
Hepatic or cardiac involvement in atypical presentations
reference.prognosis: Long-term outlook is dominated by renal disease and progressive visual loss, compounded by the metabolic consequences of obesity; the atypical and oligogenic forms show wide variability, so prognosis must be individualised.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis when a cardinal feature is absent in an atypical case
Relying on a single gene result and missing an oligogenic contribution
Overlooking renal disease, an important cause of morbidity
Failing to reassess the diagnosis as the phenotype evolves through childhood
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Manage hyperphagia and obesity with dietary, activity and behavioural measures, and consider the melanocortin-4 receptor pathway agonist setmelanotide for Bardet-Biedl-associated obesity
Provide ophthalmological care for rod-cone dystrophy with low-vision aids, support and monitoring of visual function
Nephrology surveillance and management of renal structural and functional disease, progressing to renal replacement therapy where needed
Screen for and treat metabolic and endocrine complications including type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia and hypogonadism, with hormone replacement where indicated
Surgical correction of postaxial polydactyly and developmental and educational support for learning difficulties
Coordinate lifelong multidisciplinary care across ophthalmology, nephrology, endocrinology and clinical genetics
Provide genetic counselling covering autosomal recessive and oligogenic or triallelic inheritance, with family testing and cascade screening
